title: Maximizing Water Held Between Two Lines

concept: Given an array of non-negative integers representing heights of vertical lines, find two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container that holds the most water. Return the maximum amount of water the container can store.

solutions.label: Brute Force with Nested Loops
solutions.summary: Check every pair of lines and compute the area for each, tracking the maximum.

solutions.label: Two-Pointer Greedy Approach
solutions.summary: Start with pointers at both ends and move the shorter side inward, updating the maximum area at each step.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD

    subgraph Question["Which two lines hold the most water?"]

    Input --> Question
    classDef red fill:#f87171,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here is today's problem. You are given an array of non-negative integers. Each integer represents the height of a vertical line drawn at that index. Your task is to pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container. The goal is to maximize the amount of water that container can hold.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: So the water a container can hold is determined by the shorter of the two lines times the horizontal distance between them, correct? And I just need to return the maximum area, not the indices?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. The area equals the minimum of the two heights multiplied by the distance between their indices. Return only the maximum area as an integer. The array will have at least two elements, and all values are non-negative.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. What about edge cases? If all heights are zero, the answer is zero. If all heights are equal, the widest pair wins. And the lines themselves have no thickness, so we cannot tilt the container.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That is right. You can assume the array length can be up to one hundred thousand, so efficiency matters.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. Let me summarize: given an integer array of heights, find the pair of lines that maximizes the area, which is the minimum height of the two lines times the distance between them. Let me start with a straightforward approach.

sections.title: Brute Force with Nested Loops
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph BF["Brute Force: Check All Pairs"]
        S["Heights: 1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7"]:::blue
        P1["i=0, j=1: min 1,8 × 1 = 1"]:::blue
        P2["i=0, j=2: min 1,6 × 2 = 2"]:::blue
        P3["..."]:::blue
        P4["i=1, j=8: min 8,7 × 7 = 49 ★"]:::blue
        P5["i=1, j=6: min 8,8 × 5 = 40"]:::blue
        P6["Total pairs: 36"]
    end
    S --> P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P6
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest idea is to try every possible pair of lines. I use two nested loops. The outer loop picks the left line at index i, and the inner loop picks the right line at index j, where j is greater than i. For each pair, I compute the area and track the maximum.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me walk through a small example. For the array one, eight, six, two, five, four, eight, three, seven, I check all thirty-six pairs. When i equals one and j equals eight, the area is the minimum of eight and seven, times seven, which gives forty-nine. That turns out to be the maximum.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What is the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The time complexity is O of n-squared because of the nested loops. Space is O of one since I only store the maximum value. This works for small inputs, but with up to one hundred thousand elements, n-squared is too slow. I need a better strategy.

sections.title: Two-Pointer Greedy Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph TP["Two-Pointer on: 1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7"]
        S1["left=0 right=8: min 1,7 × 8 = 8 → move left"]:::purple
        S2["left=1 right=8: min 8,7 × 7 = 49 → move right"]:::purple
        S3["left=1 right=7: min 8,3 × 6 = 18 → move right"]:::purple
        S4["left=1 right=6: min 8,8 × 5 = 40 → move either"]:::purple
        S5["... continue until pointers meet"]:::purple
        S6["Max area found: 49"]:::purple
    end
    S1 --> S2 --> S3 --> S4 --> S5 --> S6
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can do much better with a two-pointer technique. I place one pointer at the start and one at the end of the array. The key insight is that the width is maximized when the pointers are farthest apart. The only way to possibly find a larger area is to increase the height, so I move the pointer pointing to the shorter line inward.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Using the same array: left starts at index zero with height one, right at index eight with height seven. The area is one times eight, which is eight. Since the left side is shorter, I move left to index one. Now the area is the minimum of eight and seven, times seven, giving forty-nine. The right side is shorter, so I move right inward.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Why is it safe to discard the shorter side? Could we miss a better answer?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Great question. If the left line is shorter, then pairing it with any line closer than the current right pointer would give both a smaller width and a height still limited by the left line. So no combination with the shorter line can beat the current area. We safely discard it.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: We continue moving pointers inward until they meet. The time complexity is O of n because each pointer moves at most n times total. Space is O of one. This is optimal for this problem.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison["Approach Comparison"]
        BF["Brute Force\nTime: O n-squared\nSpace: O 1"]:::blue
        TP["Two-Pointer\nTime: O n\nSpace: O 1"]:::purple
    end
    BF -- "Optimize with greedy insight" --> TP
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,color:#000
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,color:#000

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice work. Let us recap. The brute-force approach checks all pairs in O of n-squared time. The two-pointer technique uses a greedy strategy to achieve O of n time with constant space.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key takeaway is recognizing that moving the shorter pointer inward is safe because keeping it cannot produce a larger area. This greedy reasoning is what makes the two-pointer approach both correct and efficient.
